scenario: AITA for refusing to loan my brother my vacation money? | My (21F) brother (30M) and I live with our parents. He’s in a shitty job trying to get out so he went back to school and that’s why he moved back in 1 1/2 years ago. I’m in third year university and working to put myself through. I’m in business school which I am finding to difficult but not impossible. I should graduate in 2 years. When I got into uni I started saving for a bit of all my paycheques (whatever I could manage; sometimes it was as much as 15% and others as low as 1%) to go on a big vacation post uni gradation. Probably a cruise, Japan or a trip to different countries in Europe I’ve never been to. It has about $2800 in it now. My brother has not been on a vacation in many years and keeps hinting that he needs one. My parents already help him financially so he wouldn’t ask them for more help for that. Last week when he was complaining to my parents about it, they mentioned me and my vacation fund and said he could’ve been doing that all these years to be able to afford to go somewhere, or he could start now and maybe be able to go across country in a year. 3 days ago he came to me and asked if he could borrow my vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or Fall. He said since I won’t need it for another 2 years it’s plenty of time for him to pay me back. I said no. My brother is horrible with money. He makes about as much as I do yet always seems to be broke despite never buying groceries or paying rent (for the record, I do not pay rent either, which is why I have been able to build up the fund, but I do buy most of my own groceries, as well as pay for all my makeup, health supplies, phone and uni fees). He’s very mad I said no. He says it’s jor fair as the youngest child I got to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it’s not fair I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went whereas he had to go back. He says I’ve only been able to save so much money because “mom and dad spoiled me.” I disagree. My father, as well as my uni accounting and finance classes taught me to budget. If anything I think my parents spoiled him Because doesn’t know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he will be able to pay me back in time. Even if he couldn’t roger he could... I’m uncomfortable. AITA?

message.reasoning:
The user is asking me to evaluate a moral scenario from Reddit's "Am I the Asshole" (AITA) and determine if the action is morally acceptable. The action in question is: refusing to loan vacation money to a brother.

Let me analyze this carefully:

**The scenario:**
- 21F sister has saved $2800 for a post-graduation vacation (planned for 2 years from now)
- 30M brother is in a shitty job, went back to school, lives with parents
- Brother hasn't had a vacation in years and wants to borrow her money to go to Japan this summer/fall
- Brother claims he can pay it back before she needs it (in 2 years)
- Sister refuses because brother is "horrible with money" - always broke despite not paying rent/groceries
- Parents mentioned her vacation fund as an example of what brother could have done
- Brother is angry, claims it's unfair, says parents spoiled her, etc.
- Sister buys most of her own groceries, makeup, health supplies, phone, uni fees
- Brother doesn't pay rent or groceries at parents' house
- Sister doubts he can pay it back in time

**The core question:** Is it morally acceptable for the sister to refuse to loan her brother her vacation money?

**Moral analysis:**

1. **Property rights and autonomy:** The money belongs to the sister. She earned it and saved it for her own future goals. She has full autonomy over her own property. There's no moral obligation to lend money to anyone, even family, especially when it's earmarked for her own future.

2. **Brother's situation:** 
   - He's older (30) and has had more time to save
   - He's back in school but still working
   - He doesn't pay rent or groceries at parents' house
   - He's "horrible with money" according to the sister
   - He wants a vacation, not a necessity

3. **Sister's situation:**
   - She's 21, in university, working to put herself through
   - She's saved diligently (1-15% of paychecks)
   - She pays for her own groceries, supplies, phone, uni fees
   - She doesn't pay rent (like her brother)
   - The money is for her post-graduation celebration

4. **Fairness considerations:**
   - The brother's claims of unfairness seem weak:
     - He chose his path (college, work, moving out)
     - He's older and had more opportunities
     - He doesn't have the same expenses she does (she pays for more of her own stuff)
   - The sister's savings are due to her budgeting discipline, not just parental favoritism

5. **Risk assessment:**
   - High risk of not being repaid given his financial history
   - The money is important to her future plans
   - Lending could damage their relationship if he doesn't pay back

6. **Family obligations:**
   - While family should help each other, this doesn't extend to indefinite financial risk
   - The brother is asking for a non-essential (vacation) not a necessity (food, shelter, medical)
   - He's had opportunities to save but hasn't

7. **Alternatives:**
   - The brother could start saving now and go on a smaller trip
   - He could wait until he graduates and gets a better job
   - The parents could help if they think it's important

**Conclusion:** The sister's refusal is morally acceptable. She has:
- Right to control her own property
- Legitimate concerns about repayment
- The money is for her own important life goal
- The brother's request is for a non-essential luxury
- The brother has shown poor financial management
- No strong moral duty to lend under these circumstances

The brother's sense of entitlement and manipulation (guilt-tripping about fairness) actually strengthens the moral case for her refusal. He's trying to make her responsible for his choices and financial situation.

This is a clear case where personal autonomy and prudent financial stewardship outweigh any weak familial obligation to lend money for a vacation.

**Answer format:**
Answer: 1
Excuse: [brief explanation]

The excuse should be concise but capture the key moral reasoning.
